segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit to be tested by the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the tester came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘It is not on bread alone that a person will live, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written: ‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, and they will lift you up on their hands, so that you never strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Again, it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and waited on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and on those sitting in the land and shadow of death a light has dawned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left their nets and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went around the whole of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The report about him spread into the whole of Syria, and they brought to him all who were unwell, gripped by various diseases and torments, those possessed by demons, epileptics, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

notes.note: The Greek verb covers both testing someone's character and enticing them to do wrong; English has to choose. Most translations keep “tempted” here, since the devil's aim is to draw Jesus into sin. “Tested” is used because all three of Jesus' replies come from Deuteronomy 6–8, where Israel is tested in the wilderness for forty years, and because it keeps the link with “the tester” in verse 3 and “put to the test” in verse 7, which share the same Greek root.

The Greek word means literally “little wing” and refers to some projecting or elevated part of the temple complex. Exactly which part is unknown; suggestions include a corner of the outer colonnade above the Kidron valley, a parapet, or the roof edge of the sanctuary. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept, but it should not be pictured as a spire.

Many later manuscripts read “Get behind me, Satan,” matching Jesus' words to Peter in 16:23. The shorter reading is found in the earliest witnesses and is generally judged original, the longer one being an assimilation to the later passage.

Most translations say John was “arrested” or “put in prison,” which is what happened. The Greek verb means simply “handed over,” and Matthew goes on to use the same verb repeatedly for what will happen to Jesus. Keeping the literal sense lets the reader hear that parallel between John's fate and Jesus'.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one Greek word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context. The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2; Galilee lay on Israel's northern edge, bordered by non-Jewish populations.

“Repent” in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word here carries the prophets' call to “return” to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

Matthew's phrase is plural in Greek, “the kingdom of the heavens,” reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking. Most translations flatten it to “kingdom of heaven.” The plural is kept because a first-century hearer would have noticed this Semitic turn of phrase.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for welcome news, especially a public announcement such as a victory or a ruler's accession. “Gospel” has become a religious technical term and a name for a kind of book, neither of which the first hearers would have heard here. Many modern translations also use “good news,” while others keep “gospel” for continuity.

The Greek word means literally “moonstruck,” reflecting the ancient belief that certain recurring afflictions were governed by the moon. The symptoms described under the same word in Matthew 17:15 resemble seizures, so most modern translations render it “epileptics.” The Greek does not make a medical diagnosis in the modern sense.

The Decapolis (“Ten Cities”) was a group of largely Greek-speaking, predominantly non-Jewish cities, most of them east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. Its mention suggests that Jesus' reputation reached beyond Jewish territory.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “tempt” and “test” across the Gospels, James, Hebrews and the Lord's Prayer noun πειρασμός, and readers will be misled if the English varies without a rule.
It ranges from bowing in homage to a superior to worship of God, and translations vary between “worship,” “bow down” and “pay homage,” especially when Jesus is the object.
“Gospel” versus “good news” recurs across the Gospels and Paul and needs a single policy, together with the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι.
Rendered variously as “arrest,” “betray,” “deliver” and “hand over,” which hides a deliberate thread linking John, Jesus and the disciples.
“Preach” now suggests a sermon in church while the Greek means a herald's public announcement; the choice between “preach” and “proclaim” should be uniform.
